2027-07-16.title: Friday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time · Our Lady of Mount Carmel
readings: When I see the blood, I will pass over you
I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord
I desire mercy and not sacrifice
2027-07-16.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I), with the optional memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel (white), much loved in India and in Kerala, where the brown scapular is widely worn. The weekday readings above are shown; the Mass of the memorial has its own proper readings, which are Zechariah 2:14–17 (NRSV 2:10–13), Luke 1:46–55 (the Magnificat) and Matthew 12:46–50. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-16.verse: Elijah went up to the top of Carmel … At the seventh time he said, “Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea.”
theo: Today's first reading is the last night in Egypt, and it is the most important night in the Old Testament. Nine plagues have fallen; “the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.” Now God gives Moses and Aaron the instructions for the night of liberation. First, a new calendar: “This month shall mark for you the beginning of months.” The liberation of the people becomes the beginning of the year. Then, a meal in each home: “a lamb for each family,” “without blemish, a year-old male,” kept until the fourteenth day and then slaughtered at twilight by the whole assembly. Some of its blood is put “on the two doorposts and the lintel” of the house. It is eaten “with unleavened bread and bitter herbs,” in haste: “your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand.” “It is the passover of the Lord.” The word means passing over: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague shall destroy you.” And then the command that turns an event into a tradition: “This day shall be a day of remembrance for you. You shall celebrate it as a festival to the Lord; throughout your generations you shall observe it as a perpetual ordinance.” Jews celebrate this meal today, in every generation, in the Seder; and the Church, from the beginning, has seen in the unblemished lamb a picture of Christ: John the Baptist calls him “the Lamb of God,” and Paul writes, “our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The psalm is the answer of someone who has been saved: “What shall I return to the Lord for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.” We say these words at the Mass, because they are the grateful prayer of the Passover and the Eucharist.

In the Gospel the disciples walk through the grainfields on the sabbath and, being hungry, pluck some heads of grain. The Pharisees object: “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the sabbath.” Plucking grain was counted as reaping, one of the kinds of work forbidden on the day of rest. Jesus does not abolish the sabbath; he explains it, with three arguments from Scripture. First, David and his men, when hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which only the priests might eat. Need and mercy come before the letter. Second, the priests in the temple work on the sabbath, offering the sacrifices, and are guiltless: the service of God takes precedence. Then the astonishing sentence: “I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.” He means himself. And then he quotes the prophet Hosea: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” Mercy is the key that opens the law. The passage ends with a claim of authority: “the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.” The Passover lamb and this Gospel meet in the same truth: the God who passes over his people in mercy has come among them in his Son, who is greater than the temple, greater than the sabbath, and who will be the Lamb.

Today the Church also remembers Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and the day has its own beauty. Carmel is a mountain ridge by the sea in the Holy Land, near present-day Haifa, and its name is bound up with Elijah. On Carmel he called down fire on the altar and challenged the prophets of Baal; and at the end of the drought he “went up to the top of Carmel; there he bowed himself down upon the earth and put his face between his knees,” and sent his servant to look toward the sea. Six times there was nothing. “At the seventh time he said, ‘Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea.’” In a little while the heavens grew black with rain. Christian tradition, and the Carmelites in particular, have seen in that little cloud a sign of Mary, a small and humble figure out of whom came the rain of grace, her Son. In the twelfth century hermits settled on Mount Carmel and built a chapel in honour of Our Lady, and they became the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, who gave the Church Teresa of Avila, John of the Cross and Thérèse of Lisieux, and whose spirituality also shaped, in Kerala, the religious family of St Kuriakose Elias Chavara. The proper readings for today are the Magnificat, in which Mary sings “the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name”; the prophet Zechariah's words, “Sing and rejoice, O daughter Zion! For lo, I will come and dwell in your midst”; and the Gospel in which Jesus says that his true family are those who do the will of his Father. Mary is the first and best of them: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). The brown scapular, a small piece of cloth worn on the shoulders, is a sign of belonging to Mary and of the wish to follow her way. A tradition says that Our Lady gave it to the English Carmelite St Simon Stock in 1251, though historians are cautious about the details. The Church teaches that the scapular is a sacramental: a sign that helps us to pray, to trust Mary's care and to imitate her, not a charm. Salvation is always Christ's gift. In July, when Kerala watches the sky for the monsoon, a cloud bringing rain is a good picture of Mary: small, humble, and carrying the water of life.
outline: Ask: when everything seems dry, what do you do while you wait for the rain?
Point 1 · When I see the blood
The Passover night and the Lamb without blemish.
Something greater than the temple is here; the Lord of the sabbath.
Elijah on Carmel, persistent prayer, and Mary as the small cloud that brings the rain.
Point 4 · Do whatever he tells you
Mary the first disciple, and the scapular as a sign of belonging.
“Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
live: Choose one need that is still unanswered and bring it to God every day this week, even seven times, without giving up.
If you have a scapular, wear it today and offer it as a promise to imitate Mary's yes. If not, say a Hail Mary at midday with the words: Mother, teach me to do whatever he tells me.
2027-07-16.prayer: Lord God, on the night of the Passover you saw the blood on the doorposts and passed over your people. Through Christ, our Passover lamb, you have saved us and given us the cup of salvation. Teach us mercy rather than the letter. Lord Jesus, you who are greater than the temple, and lord of the sabbath, receive our thanks. Father, as Elijah looked to the sea and saw a little cloud, so we look to Our Lady of Mount Carmel and see in her the one who bore your Son and who did your will. Through her prayers, make us faithful in waiting, humble in service and generous in mercy. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest takes the cup, and we remember Psalm 116: “I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.” The Mass is the Passover of the New Covenant: Christ, the Lamb without blemish, whose blood saves us, is offered, and we eat the Lamb at his table. “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.” Mary stands close to this mystery: she gave him his body and blood, and at the foot of the cross she stood united with his sacrifice.

quick: On the night of the Passover each family takes an unblemished lamb, marks the doorposts with its blood and eats it in haste; God passes over their homes.
The disciples pluck grain on the sabbath; Jesus replies that something greater than the temple is here, that God desires mercy, and that he is lord of the sabbath.
On Mount Carmel Elijah prays seven times and sees a little cloud rising from the sea; Mary, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, is the one who bore the rain of grace.
2027-07-16.action: Pray one Hail Mary for a need that is still unanswered, and add: Mother, help me to wait like Elijah.
2027-07-16.question: Do I keep going back to prayer, like Elijah's servant who looked seven times, or do I stop after the first “There is nothing”?
kidsaint: A long time ago, on a mountain by the sea called Mount Carmel, a prophet named Elijah prayed for rain. He sent his helper to look at the sky, and the helper came back six times: nothing! The seventh time he said: I see a tiny cloud, as small as a man's hand! Soon the rain came. Many centuries later, Christian hermits lived on the same mountain and built a little chapel for Mary. They are called the Carmelites. Some people wear a small brown cloth, called a scapular, to remember that Mary loves them and that they want to follow her.

family.explain: Elijah was praying for rain. There had been no rain for a long time and everything was dry. He told his helper: look at the sea! Six times the helper said: nothing! But Elijah did not give up. The seventh time the helper saw a small cloud, no bigger than a hand. Soon the sky was dark and the rain came pouring down. Mary is like that little cloud: small and humble, but she brought Jesus to us. And Jesus is the one who gives us everything we need.
family.intention: We pray for rain where it is needed, and where there is too much rain, and for all farmers and fishermen. We thank Mary for being our mother, and ask her to help us to do whatever Jesus tells us.
family.ask: Ask: “What are we waiting for? Shall we pray for it every day this week, like Elijah, and not give up?” Say a Hail Mary together.

illus: A woman in a coastal village near Kollam used to sit on her veranda every evening from the first week of June, looking at the sky. Her husband was a fisherman and the sea was rough. She told her granddaughter once that when the sky looks empty, she says her rosary and looks for the first little cloud, and that Our Lady, who knows what it is to wait and to hope, always sends one. One evening the girl saw a cloud no bigger than her own hand, and the old woman smiled and said: that is the beginning. Soon the rain came, and the next morning her husband's boat was back at the shore. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord, Lamb of God, you are our Passover. Our Lady of Mount Carmel, mother of the Lamb, pray with us. Amen.
share: When I see the blood, I will pass over you (Exodus 12:13). Where have I experienced God passing over me, sparing me from something worse?
I will lift up the cup of salvation (Psalm 116:13). How can I bring my thanksgiving at the Mass to a new depth this week?
Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person's hand (1 Kings 18:44). What small sign of hope is God showing me in a time of waiting?
pm.resp: I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that she may keep the Passover of Christ with gratitude and mercy.
For the Carmelite family, in Kerala and throughout the world, and for all who wear the scapular.
For farmers and fishermen, and for a monsoon that brings life and not harm.
For all who are waiting and praying for something for a long time, that they may not give up.
For our group, that following Mary we may do whatever Jesus tells us.
pm.close: Father, you gave us Christ, the Lamb, and Mary, his mother and ours. Through her intercession and example, lead us to your Son who lives and reigns with you for ever and ever. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, imagine the night of the Passover. In every Hebrew home a family is eating in haste, shoes on, staff in hand. On the doorpost is the blood of a lamb without blemish. And God says: when I see the blood, I will pass over you (Exodus 12:13). Every year, for three thousand years, the Jewish people have kept that night. And we, in the Mass, keep our Passover: Christ is the Lamb without blemish, his blood saves us, and every time we receive him we pass from slavery to life. Let us remember what Paul says: our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).

In the Gospel the disciples are hungry and pluck some grain, and the Pharisees say: it is not lawful! And Jesus answers with a sentence that should wake us up: I desire mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 12:7). Rules matter; worship matters. But if a rule makes us forget a hungry person, we have lost its point. Something greater than the temple is here, he says (Matthew 12:6). It is he himself, the Lord of the sabbath. Mercy is the key to the whole law.

Today we also remember Our Lady of Mount Carmel. On Mount Carmel the prophet Elijah prayed for rain, and he said to his servant: look toward the sea. Six times: there is nothing. The seventh time: a little cloud no bigger than a person's hand (1 Kings 18:44). Dear friends, sometimes our prayer feels like that. We look and see nothing. Elijah teaches us to go back, again and again. And the tradition of the Church saw in that little cloud Mary: a humble young woman from Nazareth, no bigger than a hand in the eyes of the world, and out of her came Jesus, the rain of grace for the whole world.

The Carmelites took Mary as their mother and their model. They wear the scapular, a small cloth, as a sign that they belong to her and want to live as she lived. And what was her life? Here am I, the servant of the Lord (Luke 1:38). And at Cana: do whatever he tells you (John 2:5). Today let us ask Our Lady of Carmel to teach us that, to pray like Elijah, to be merciful like Jesus and to say yes like her. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago on a mountain called Mount Carmel there was a prophet named Elijah. There was no rain, and everything was dry. Elijah prayed. He told his helper: look at the sea! The helper looked and said: nothing! Elijah said: look again! Seven times! The seventh time the helper saw a little cloud, as small as a hand. And then came the rain! We remember Mary today as Our Lady of Carmel. She is like the little cloud: small and humble, and she brought us Jesus. Some people wear a little brown scapular to remember that Mary is our mother. Let us say a Hail Mary and ask her to help us to wait and pray like Elijah, and not give up.

intro: Theme: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord.”
The blood on the doorposts and the Lamb, mercy greater than sacrifice, and the little cloud over Carmel that is Mary.

sub: The first month, the first night.
A day of remembrance for ever.
q: The blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you live: when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague shall destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.
Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch, as you really are unleavened. For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.
points.apply: At the next Mass, listen to the words “Behold the Lamb of God” and receive Holy Communion as a Passover.

sub: David and the bread of the Presence.
q: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. For the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
points.apply: This week, let mercy win over a rule once: feed someone, forgive someone, or help someone in need.

sub: Six times nothing, the seventh time a cloud.
Mary, small and humble, who brought the rain of grace.
q: At the seventh time he said, “Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea.”
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
points.apply: Pray daily this week, and do not stop at the first “nothing”: go back seven times if you need to.

sub: The scapular as a sign of belonging.
Hearing the word and keeping it.
q: Sing and rejoice, O daughter Zion! For lo, I will come and dwell in your midst, says the Lord.
But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
points.apply: Say a Hail Mary each morning this week, asking: Mother, show me what he wants me to do today.

concl: God passes over his people at the Passover; in Christ, the Lamb, he has saved us, and he desires mercy more than sacrifice.
As a little cloud brought rain to Carmel, Mary brought Jesus to the world, and she teaches us to hear the word and keep it.
2027-07-16.resolve: Each day this week say a Hail Mary to Our Lady of Mount Carmel for a need that is still unanswered, and do one act of mercy.
